title: Why I built VooSquare
excerpt: I spent years paying for lessons the expensive way. VooSquare is the home I wish I had when I started buying traffic.
body: Before I bought my first ad, I taught economics and mathematics. I spent my days explaining compound interest, opportunity cost and why you never put money into something you cannot measure. Then I started running paid traffic and ignored almost every one of those lessons.

I paid for courses that were mostly screenshots. I paid for tools that did one small job each and did not talk to each other. I ran ads that brought cheap leads and no deposits, and I kept running them because the dashboard looked green. I burnt money the wrong way, many times, before I learned what actually works.
What I learned the hard way

Over time, the business at Zedapex grew into a large paid-traffic operation across Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Ghana and Cameroon, in the trading and iGaming verticals. The lessons that made the difference were simple, and almost none of them were about secret targeting.
Treat traffic as capital. Every dollar of spend should buy something you can measure and grow.
Price every lead before you buy it. Payout times FTD rate tells you the most a join is worth.
Send the platform real signals. If you report clicks, it finds clickers.
Keep a steady flow of new creatives, because every winner wears out.
Follow up for weeks after the join. That is where most leads pay you back.

I call this traffic banking. It is the way a banker looks at a loan: what does it cost, what does it return, and how fast does the money come back? Once I started running campaigns like that, my decisions got calmer and my results got easier to repeat.

Every serious buyer I know runs on the same stack: an offer, creatives, tracking, a Telegram funnel, a way to answer leads, a way to follow up and a way to get paid. Most of us glue it together from a dozen tools, a dozen logins and a lot of WhatsApp groups where the good advice gets lost under the noise.

We built the Voo tools at Zedapex to fix the gaps we kept hitting in our own campaigns. Spyvoo shows the live Facebook and Instagram ads that have run for months, and why they work. Joinvoo tracks every real Telegram join and deposit and sends them to Meta, TikTok and Snapchat server-side. Vooads makes creatives in every size and in Pidgin, Swahili and French. Replyvoo answers every chat in seconds. Castvoo runs broadcasts and follow-ups. Affleego lists CPA and RevShare deals. Landvoo and Gatevoo are on the way.

VooSquare is where all of it lives. One Voo ID opens every tool. Next to the tools sit a community of people doing the same work, an Academy with the lessons I wish someone had taught me, and a blog with playbooks you can use the same week you read them.
I built the place I needed when I was burning money and did not know why.

A lot of it, and it stays free. Your Voo ID, access to every tool's free offer, the free community rooms, the free Academy courses including Traffic Banking 101, the blog and support for every tool. You can learn the whole foundation of traffic banking without paying VooSquare anything.

Premium is $20 a month and it is for operators who are scaling. It opens the premium rooms (Buyers' Lounge, Scaling Desk, Offer Drops and Creative Reviews), every Academy course including the advanced tracks on scaling, offers and running a team, and a monthly live campaign breakdown with me, with replays. You also get templates and playbooks, priority support, the Premium badge and early access to new tools.
One thing VooSquare will never do is hold your money for the tools. There is no wallet and no top-up here. Each tool handles its own billing. VooSquare only charges for Premium and for paid rooms.

Come with your real numbers. Share what worked and what failed. Follow the law and the ad platform's rules in every country you run, especially in trading and gambling. Nobody here will promise you income, and you should be careful of anyone who does. What we can promise is better tools, honest lessons and a room full of people who do this work every day.

title: The cheap lead that cost me the most
excerpt: For a long time I trusted cost per lead over real joins. Here is how that habit burnt money, and the checks I use now.
body: There is a campaign I still think about. The cost per lead was the lowest I had ever seen. I screenshotted it. I raised the budget. I told people about it. And at the end of the month it had produced almost nothing I could bank.
I am not going to put numbers on it, because the exact figures do not matter and I do not want anyone anchoring on them. The pattern matters, because I see buyers repeat it every week.

The campaign was optimising for leads, and it found them. Lots of them. What it found were people who tapped the button easily: curious scrollers, accidental taps, some accounts that were clearly not real people, and many who joined the channel and never read a single post.

The ad platform did exactly what I asked. I asked for cheap leads, so it went where leads were cheapest. The people most likely to deposit were not in that pool, and the cheaper the leads got, the further the algorithm moved away from them.
The algorithm did exactly what I asked. I was asking for the wrong thing.
Why the dashboard lied to me

Cost per lead measures the price of an action. It says nothing about what that action is worth. A lead that never deposits is worth zero, whatever it cost. I was reading the price tag and ignoring the product.
There were three gaps in how I was tracking at the time:
I was counting clicks on the join button as leads, so many leads never actually joined.
I could not tie deposits back to the ad set that brought them, so the cheap ad set and the good ad set looked the same in my sheet.
I was sending the platform an event that happened often and meant little, so it optimised for volume.

Today I do not look at cost per lead on its own. I look at cost per real join, the share of those joins that deposit, and cost per FTD by ad set. If a campaign is cheap at the top and empty at the bottom, it gets switched off no matter how good the screenshot looks.
Price the lead before launch: payout times FTD rate gives the most a join is worth.
Count only real joins, tracked with a unique invite link per click.
Send real joins or deposits to the platform server-side, so it learns from people who act.
Read cost per FTD by ad set every day, and compare cohorts by the week they joined.
Filter duplicates and people who leave straight away before reporting them as conversions.
The cost was more than the spend

The money spent on that campaign was the smaller loss. The bigger loss was time. I spent weeks scaling something that could not work, while campaigns that looked more expensive on the surface and actually made deposits got less budget. I also trained the account on bad signals, which took time to undo.
That is why I tell every new buyer the same thing: a cheap lead is only cheap if it pays you back. If you cannot see whether it pays you back, you do not know whether it is cheap.
If this sounds like your account

Start with the Tracking that tells the truth course in the Academy. It covers unique invite links, server-side events and how to choose the right optimisation event. Then go back to your sheet and add one column next to cost per lead: cost per FTD. Watch how differently your ad sets rank.

title: Traffic banking explained
excerpt: Traffic banking treats lead acquisition as capital. Here is what that means in practice, with the formulas and habits behind it.
body: Traffic banking is the way we run paid traffic at Zedapex. The idea is short: treat every dollar you spend on ads as capital you lend out and expect back with a return. Everything else follows from that.

A bank does not lend money and hope. It knows the rate, checks the borrower, lends small first, and lends more only when the last loan came back. Media buying works better when you think the same way.
Before you buy a single lead, work out what one is worth. The formula is payout per FTD (first-time deposit) multiplied by your FTD rate, the share of joins that deposit.

Example: if a network pays $60 per FTD and 4 in every 100 joins deposit, each join is worth $2.40 to you. That is break-even. To keep a margin, bid below it. At 70% of break-even, your target cost per join is $1.68.
If you do not have your own FTD rate yet, start with a careful estimate and replace it with real data as soon as you have a few weeks of results.

The ad platform finds more people like the ones you report. If you report clicks, it finds people who click. If you report real joins or deposits from your server, it looks for people who join and deposit. Choosing what you report is one of the biggest decisions you make.

New campaigns, creatives and geos get small, fixed test budgets with written kill rules. Winners earn more budget in steps. Many buyers raise winners by about 20% at a time and wait a day or two between raises. Losers are switched off by rule, before hope gets a vote.
Scaling is lending more to a borrower who has repaid.

Most leads do not deposit on the day they join. The return on your spend comes from what happens next: a fast welcome, useful daily content, quick replies in the inbox, and a planned follow-up over two weeks or more. Buying a join and then going quiet is like lending money and never sending a statement.
A banker reads the books every day. You should too. These are the numbers that matter:
Spend, by ad set and by geo.
Real joins and cost per real join.
Revenue and ROAS (revenue divided by spend).
Cohort value: what each week's joins have returned at day 7 and day 30.

Your ad accounts, pages, pixel history and payment methods are the vault. Without them nothing runs. Use two-factor on every admin, keep at least two trusted admins, pay bills on time, keep a backup payment method attached, and stay inside the ad platform's rules and the law of every country you run in. For trading and gambling offers, check both in every geo before spending.
What traffic banking will not do

Traffic banking will not guarantee profit. Campaigns lose. Offers change. Accounts get restricted. What it gives you is a way of making decisions so that losses stay small and planned, and wins can be repeated. It also makes your results easier to explain to a partner, a network manager or yourself six months from now.

Open a sheet with five columns: date, spend, joins, FTDs and payouts. Fill it every day for a week. At the end of the week, divide payouts by spend. That number, your return per dollar, is the first line of your ledger. Then take the free Traffic Banking 101 course in the Academy, which walks through each of these ideas with worked examples.

title: The join-request funnel, step by step
excerpt: Join requests give you a first message, tracking per link and a chance to filter junk. Here is how to set one up from ad to approval.
body: Most Telegram funnels use one open invite link in every ad. Someone taps, joins instantly, and disappears into the member count. You do not know which ad brought them, you cannot greet them personally, and bots join as easily as people.
A join-request funnel fixes all three. It adds one tap for the user and gives you a lot of control in return.

When you create an invite link, you can switch on admin approval. Anyone who opens that link sends a request to join instead of joining straight away. A bot that is an admin of the channel receives each request with the user's details and the link they used. The bot can send the person a short message while the request is pending, then approve it.

Create a fresh invite link for each visitor on your landing page and store their click ID next to it. When that link is used, you know exactly which ad, ad set and campaign brought the person. This is what turns a member count into cost per join by ad.
Every link you create should have admin approval on. This is what gives your bot a moment with each person before they are inside the channel.
Step 3: send a short first message

Telegram gives the bot a short window to message the person while the request is pending. Use it well. Keep it to two or three lines: greet them by name, confirm what they joined for and ask one easy question.
Every join request is a knock on the door. Answer it like you paid for it.

Before approving, run quick checks. Has this user ID already joined through another link? Are many requests arriving from one source in a few seconds? Is the account empty and brand new? Some odd-looking accounts belong to real people, so rejecting all of them is too harsh. Hold back their join events from the ad platform until they look real.
Approve fast. A request left pending for hours feels broken to the person who sent it.
Step 5: send the join as a server event

Once a real person is approved, send the join to Meta, TikTok or Snapchat through their server-side APIs, tied to the original click. Now the ad platform learns from real joins instead of clicks on a button. Joinvoo does this part for you, or you can build it with your own bot and database.
Tag each person by their answer to the first question and start the matching follow-up sequence. Beginners get the basics first. Experienced users get the faster path.
A bot added as admin of the channel, with permission to manage invite links.
A unique invite link per click, with admin approval switched on.
The click ID stored next to each link.
A first message of two or three lines with one question.
Duplicate and burst checks before approving.
Each real join sent server-side to the ad platform.
A follow-up sequence for each answer.
Approving first and messaging later. Once approved, the bot may lose its chance to message unless the person starts it.
Long first messages with several links. Keep it short.
Reporting every request to the ad platform, including duplicates and bots.
Testing with ad traffic. Test the full flow with a second Telegram account first.

Stay within Telegram's rules throughout: no mass unsolicited messages, no fake members and quick action on reports. The Telegram funnels that deposit course in the Academy covers each step in more detail, including the welcome message and a 14-day follow-up plan.

title: Kill rules: decide before you launch
excerpt: The hardest time to switch off an ad is when you are watching it. Write the rule first and let the numbers make the call.
body: Every buyer has kept an ad running longer than they should. The numbers were bad, but yesterday looked a little better, or the creative felt strong, or you had already spent so much that switching it off felt like admitting a loss. That is how small losses become large ones.
A kill rule is a decision you make before launch, when you are calm, about when an ad set gets switched off. Once it is written, the decision on the day is just reading a number.
What a kill rule looks like
A good kill rule has three parts: a metric, a threshold and an amount of spend or time. The spend part matters, because judging too early is as bad as judging too late.
Example: if an ad set spends 2 times the target CPA with zero FTDs, switch it off.
Example: if cost per real join is 50% above your maximum for 3 days in a row, switch it off.
Example: if CTR is below your floor after 1,000 impressions, switch off the ad.
Example: if frequency is rising and CTR has fallen by a third from its peak, refresh the creative.
These are examples. Your thresholds should come from your own offer, your payout and your history.

You cannot write a kill rule without a target, and you cannot set a target without knowing what a lead is worth. Payout per FTD multiplied by your FTD rate gives the most a join is worth to you. Your target cost per join sits below that, with room for profit. Your target CPA is the payout minus your other costs per FTD, less the margin you want to keep.

Kill rules stop losses. Scale rules stop you from raising budgets on one lucky day. A scale rule says when a winner gets more budget, how much more, and how long you wait before the next raise. Many buyers raise winning budgets by about 20% at a time and wait a day or two between raises. Treat that as a starting point and learn what your account handles well.
Apply them the same way every day

Rules only work if they are applied consistently. Pick a time of day. Pull the same numbers. Give every ad set one of three verdicts: kill, hold or scale. Write down what you did and why. On a team, every buyer uses the same rules, and the daily report shows which rules were applied.

Sometimes the data is wrong. A postback is delayed, tracking broke for a few hours, or a payment failure paused delivery. In those cases, fix the data first and then apply the rule. Do not break a rule because you like the creative or because you have a feeling about tomorrow.
Payout, FTD rate and break-even cost per join.
Target cost per join and target CPA.
Kill rule with a spend or time limit.
Scale rule: when, how much and how often.
Fill this in before your next launch and keep it at the top of your campaign sheet. Traffic Banking 101 in the Academy has a full lesson on kill and scale rules with worked examples.

title: Pidgin, Swahili or English: localising ads
excerpt: The language of an ad decides who feels it was made for them. How to choose a language per geo and localise properly.
body: Run the same English ad in Lagos, Nairobi, Accra, Douala and Johannesburg and you will usually see five very different results. Part of that is cost and competition. A large part is that the ad speaks to some of those people more naturally than others.
Localising means making the ad feel like it was made in and for the place it runs. Language is the biggest part, but faces, places, prices and humour matter too.
There is no single right answer per country. Cities, regions and age groups differ. These are reasonable starting points to test against each other:
Nigeria: Nigerian Pidgin and English. Pidgin often reads as more personal and direct.
Kenya: Swahili, English and Sheng, the urban mix of the two that younger audiences use.
Ghana: English, Twi and Ghanaian Pidgin.
Cameroon: French in most regions, English in the North-West and South-West, and Cameroonian Pidgin across both.
South Africa: English, with Zulu, Xhosa, Afrikaans and local slang depending on the audience.
Test the local language against English in the same ad set with the same angle. Let your cost per real join and cost per FTD decide.

A word-for-word translation keeps the structure and rhythm of the original language. Native speakers notice straight away. Localising starts from the idea and lets a native speaker say it the way they would say it to a friend.
People buy in their own words.
Write the angle and hook in plain English as a brief.
Ask a native speaker from the target area to rewrite it in their own words. Do not ask them to translate.
Record the voice-over with a voice that matches the region and age of the audience.
Use faces, streets, shops and settings that look local.
Show prices in local currency: naira, shillings, cedis, CFA francs or rand.
Test the local version against the original in the same ad set.
Keep claims honest in every language

Ad review applies in every language, and so do the law and the platform's rules on trading and gambling. A claim that would be rejected in English does not become safe in Pidgin or Swahili. Read the final script back in English to check what it really says.

Vooads writes and voices ads in Pidgin, Swahili and French and checks them against Meta's rules before you spend. It is a fast way to get several localised drafts to test. Have a native speaker listen to the final version before it goes live, especially for slang, which changes quickly.

Compare the local and English versions on hook rate, CTR, cost per real join and cost per FTD. Hook rate and CTR tell you whether people stopped and cared. Cost per FTD tells you whether the right people stopped. Sometimes a local version gets more attention and the same deposits. Sometimes it changes everything. The only way to know is to test it on your offer.
Using one Pidgin script for both Nigeria and Ghana without checking local usage.
French scripts written for France rather than Central and West Africa.
A local voice-over on top of stock footage from another continent.
Showing dollar amounts to an audience that thinks in local currency.
The Creatives that print course in the Academy has a full lesson on localising, plus hooks, formats and spotting creative fatigue.

title: Your inbox is a leaky bucket
excerpt: You paid for every lead who messages you. Slow replies, vague answers and missed handoffs let them drain away. Here is how to find the leaks.
body: Picture your funnel as a bucket. Ads pour leads in at the top. Every lead who messages you and never gets a useful answer is water running out through a hole near the bottom. Most buyers respond by pouring faster, which means buying more traffic. It is usually cheaper to fix the holes.

A lead who sends you a message is interested right now. Every minute they wait, that interest fades. They get distracted, check another channel or forget why they asked. Nights and weekends are where most teams lose the most, because nobody is online.
Measure your median first reply time, the middle value across all chats, so one slow chat does not hide how most chats went. Then cover the hours your team is offline.
Leak 2: answers with no next step

A reply that answers the question and stops there leaves the lead to decide what to do next. Many will do nothing. Every reply should end with one clear next step: read this guide, answer this question, use this link.

A beginner and an experienced user need different answers. Ask one qualifying question early, tag the answer and use the script that fits. One question is enough. Five questions upfront feels like a form, and people leave.
One good question tells you which conversation you are in.

When a lead asks if this is real, or says they lost money before, a vague reply loses them. Prepare honest answers to your five most common objections. Point to things they can check themselves. Never promise profit.

Some chats need a person: payment problems, complaints, large buyers and anything unclear. If the person who takes over cannot see the chat history, the lead has to repeat everything. If nobody gives a reply time, they assume nobody is coming.
Message your own funnel from a second account at night and on a Sunday. Time the reply.
Pull last week's chats and work out close rate: deposits divided by chats.
Read 20 chats that did not close and mark the message where each one stopped.
Count how many chats went to a human and how long those took.
Rewrite the message where most chats stop, and test it for a week.

Replyvoo's AI Closers answer every Telegram chat in seconds, at any hour, ask the qualifying question, handle common objections with your approved answers, send the payment link and hand off to your team when a chat needs a person. It also has a chat widget for your website. Whether you use it or a human team on shifts, the goal is the same: no lead waits, every reply has a next step, and handoffs keep the full context.

Example: if 300 chats a week close at 10%, that is 30 deposits. If faster replies and better scripts move close rate to 13%, that is 39 deposits from the same traffic. The ad spend stayed the same. Fewer leads you had already paid for were lost.

title: Reading an affiliate offer before you spend
excerpt: The payout is only the first line of an offer. KPIs, holds, caps and banned traffic decide what you actually get paid.
body: Two offers can show the same payout and pay you very different amounts. The difference is in the terms: what counts as a qualifying deposit, what quality the network expects, how long it holds your money, how many FTDs it will pay for and which traffic it refuses.
Read all of it before you spend. Here is what to look for and what to ask.

CPA pays a fixed amount once per qualifying FTD. RevShare pays a share of the revenue the brand earns from your players over time. Hybrid deals mix a smaller CPA with some RevShare. CPA gives faster cash flow. RevShare can earn more over time if players stay, but it pays slowly and can carry losses forward. Ask whether the RevShare has negative carryover, which deducts one month's losses from the next month's earnings.

Most CPA offers require a minimum deposit for the FTD to qualify, and some also require activity after the deposit. A lead who deposits below the minimum may not count at all. Get the exact definition in writing.

KPIs are quality targets the network checks after you send traffic. They might cover repeat deposits, activity over a set period or the share of players who stay. If you miss them, payouts can be cut or held. Ask which KPIs apply, how they are measured and over what period.

The hold is the time between an FTD and the day you are paid for it. During the hold you have already paid for the traffic. Example: at $140 a day with a 30-day hold, about $4,200 of your spend is waiting to be paid back at any time. Longer holds need more working capital.
Caps limit how many FTDs a network will pay for per day or month. Anything above the cap may be paid at a lower rate or not at all. Check caps before you scale, and ask for notice if they change.

Most offers ban some traffic sources: incentivised traffic, certain ad platforms, brand bidding, specific placements or certain countries. Sending banned traffic can void all of your payouts on that offer, including the legitimate ones.
A high payout in a geo you cannot legally run is a liability.

Trading and gambling offers must be legal in every country you target and allowed by the ad platform there. Rules differ by country and change over time. Ad platforms often restrict these categories and may require written permission. Check both before you send a single click.
What is the exact definition of a qualifying FTD, including minimum deposit?
Which KPIs apply, how are they measured and over what period?
How long is the hold, and when are payments made?
Are there daily or monthly caps, and will you notify me before they change?
Which traffic sources, placements and geos are banned?
For RevShare, is there negative carryover?
Which postback events are available, and can I pass my click ID in a sub ID?

Once you have the answers, work out your break-even. Value per join is payout multiplied by FTD rate. Break-even CPA is payout minus your other costs per FTD, such as tools, creatives and fees. Add the hold to your cash plan. If the numbers only work in a perfect week, the offer is not ready for your budget.

title: Five numbers every buyer should know daily
excerpt: Spend, cost per real join, FTD rate, cost per FTD and ROAS. Know these five every morning and most decisions get easier.
body: Ads Manager shows you dozens of columns. Most of them help you diagnose a problem once you know there is one. Five numbers tell you whether there is a problem in the first place. Check them at the same time every day, for every campaign, and write them down.

How much went out yesterday, by campaign, ad set and geo. It sounds obvious, but many problems first show up here: an ad set that spent far more than planned, a budget that did not deliver, or a payment issue that paused everything overnight.

Spend divided by real joins. Real means joins you can tie to a click and that passed your checks for duplicates and instant leavers. Compare it with your target cost per join, which comes from payout multiplied by FTD rate, less your margin.

The share of joins that made a first-time deposit. Track it by join date, because deposits keep arriving for days after people join. A falling FTD rate with a steady cost per join usually means lead quality is dropping, often because the creative or the optimisation event is attracting the wrong people.
Spend divided by FTDs. This is the number that decides most kill and scale calls. Example: $600 of spend that produced 20 FTDs is a $30 cost per FTD. Compare it with your target CPA.

Return on ad spend: revenue divided by spend. Example: $900 in payouts from $600 spend is a ROAS of 1.5, or $1.50 back for every dollar. On RevShare, ROAS keeps rising for weeks, so compare cohorts at the same age, such as day 7 and day 30.
If you do not know these five numbers this morning, you are making today's decisions on yesterday's feelings.

Read them in order. Spend tells you what went out. Cost per real join tells you what it bought. FTD rate tells you the quality of what it bought. Cost per FTD and ROAS tell you whether it paid. When one number moves, the ones before it usually tell you why.
Cost per join up, FTD rate steady: the creative is tiring or competition is rising.
Cost per join steady, FTD rate down: lead quality has dropped. Check the signal and the creative.
Both steady, ROAS down: check payouts, caps and postbacks with the network.
Everything steady, spend down: check delivery, payments and account status.

These numbers are only as good as your tracking. Use a unique invite link per click so every join ties to its ad. Pass your click ID to the network in a sub ID and receive postbacks for registrations and FTDs. Send real joins and deposits to the ad platform server-side. Joinvoo handles the Telegram part of this and, on Pro, shows deposits, ROAS and cost per FTD.
Compare with yesterday and with target.
Write down every change you made and why.
Apply your kill and scale rules once the numbers are in.
